name: Robinson Papplewick mill engine
summary: Boulton & Watt supplied an 11-horsepower rotative steam engine to Robinson's cotton mill at Papplewick around 1785–86, among the first steam engines to drive cotton spinning.
description: Boulton & Watt’s 11-horsepower sun-and-planet engine for the Robinson cotton mill, described with a 17½-inch cylinder and four-foot stroke; the surviving 1785 elevation is a documentary witness.
tier_reason: A bounded technical contribution, transmission episode or documented configuration useful within a specific history; no broad dependence claim is established.
why: The mill had relied on a waterwheel; a rotative steam engine gave power independent of the River Leen's flow.

events.caveats: The catalogue supplies the installation interpretation and dimensions; the original-resolution drawing was not inspected for this claim. No cotton-industry priority claim or exact operating start is adopted.

date.label: by 1786
date.basis: Historic England dates steam-powered cotton spinning at Papplewick to 1786; Gedling reports the Robinson factory used steam in 1785. Both are consistent with operation by the end of 1786.

events.statement: A Boulton & Watt sun-and-planet engine powered the Robinson cotton mill at Papplewick by 1786.
events.scope: The Robinson cotton mill’s Boulton & Watt 11-horsepower sun-and-planet engine, described as having a 17½-inch cylinder and a four-foot stroke; a surviving 1785 elevation is the witness.
events.caveats: Historic England dates steam-powered cotton spinning at Papplewick to 1786; Gedling dates the Robinson factory’s steam power to 1785. The archive interprets the drawing and dimensions; the drawing as built was not independently verified. No precise commissioning day or global priority is asserted.

links.statement: Confirm the link from rotative engines to mill driving, and whether water-mill practice shaped the installation.
links.caveats: Evidence needed: Boulton and Watt papers for Papplewick.
links.finding: The cited records document two distinct Boulton & Watt mill applications and a shared broad sun-and-planet method. They do not establish that the particular Soho engine was the developmental predecessor of the Papplewick engine, that the same engine or equipment moved between sites, or that the former Papplewick waterwheel shaped the installation. The accepted relationship mech-rotative-to-papplewick is from the 1781 specification to the Papplewick configuration, not from the Soho engine; it should remain distinct. No additional Soho-to-Papplewick edge is supported by the inspected passages.

links.statement: Is there any documented transmission from Roman or medieval water-mill practice to the mill engine, or only independent similarity? A documented negative is useful.
links.caveats: Evidence needed: Sources stating transmission. Similar function alone is not enough.
links.finding: The inspected sources establish water-powered mills in sixth-century Rome and an earlier waterwheel at the Papplewick mill. They do not establish a documented transmission path from the specific Roman aqueduct mills to Papplewick, its waterwheel, or its steam-engine installation. Similar function and chronological sequence do not support the proposed documented-transmission edge.
